title: Rohatsu, the fifth time
hook: the week of sitting before the awakening day
tomorrow: a monk at a hot spring meets a glowing stranger. what's the question?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kathina: a cloth woven for one, sent to the many. The rains end in gifts. Now the cold end of the year, and a night of sitting.
screen: `THE RAINS END IN GIFTS.` → `A NIGHT OF SITTING.`

segments.voice: Phones face down, alarms set for the dark: in Zen halls, the days before Rohatsu are like that, sitting long into the nights. They sit with one night in mind, and the old biographies tell it. Mara, the tempter, has spent the evening hurling storms at the man under the tree, and none of them moved him. So Mara tries a question. He says: that seat isn't yours. Who will vouch for you? Mara's whole army shouts that they'll vouch for him. The man under the tree has no one to call. So he reaches down, and touches the ground.
screen: `PHONES DOWN, ALARMS SET.` → `"THAT SEAT ISN'T YOURS."` → `AN ARMY OF WITNESSES.` → `HE TOUCHES THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: The earth answers. In the Jataka's introduction, it roars: I am his witness. And Mara's army breaks and runs. That gesture, right hand over the knee, fingertips to the ground, is the one some seated Buddha statues show: bhumisparsha, touching the earth. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't argue his case, or point up at the sky. He points down, to the plain ground under him. Then the night goes on. In the Zen telling, as dawn comes, he looks up, sees the morning star, and wakes up. So the story runs on two senses. A hand on the ground. An eye on a point of light. Here's the teaching inside Rohatsu. In this story, awakening isn't pictured as escaping the world. It happens sitting on the earth, through the body, at one ordinary dawn. Zen students keep the day by sitting, not by feasting, and some sit through the last night so they're awake when the morning star rises. In the story, the answer to Mara's question comes from the ground itself. And the detail to pass on tonight: when Mara had an army behind him, the Buddha's only witness was the dirt.
screen: `THE EARTH ANSWERS.` · `BHUMISPARSHA: TOUCHING THE EARTH.` · `A HAND DOWN, AN EYE UP.` · `AWAKE ON THE EARTH, NOT ABOVE IT.` · then, large: `THE MORNING STAR.`

segments.voice: Sit with your left hand resting in your lap. Let your right hand hang over your right knee until the fingertips touch the floor, the chair or your own leg. Feel what's under them, plain and solid, and keep them there for the whole sit, eyes soft, as if waiting for the first light.
Rohatsu: the Zen name for the day of the Buddha's awakening, kept with long nights of sitting.
For tonight: the morning star, seen by someone sitting on plain ground. Five of seven; the year turns soon.

howItsDone: Zen communities mark Rohatsu, the day of the Buddha's awakening, with a stretch of intensive sitting called sesshin, and some sit through the final night until dawn; other East Asian Buddhists mark the day at temples and at home.

sources.ref: Jataka, Nidanakatha (the introduction: Mara's challenge for the seat, the touch of the earth, the earth's witness)

notes: Nidanakatha paraphrased (Rhys Davids's 'Buddhist Birth Stories' translates it, but not quoted): Mara first sends storms (wind, rain, rocks and more) that fail to move the Bodhisatta, voiced as 'hurling storms… none of them moved him'; then Mara claims the seat; his followers cry out as his witnesses; the Bodhisatta, having no living witness, stretches his right hand toward the earth; the earth roars that it bears witness, and Mara's army flees. Confirm the wording 'I am his witness' as a paraphrase.

'Many seated Buddha statues' show the earth-touching gesture; confirm the softened wording is fine.
